deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. The previous page is an ephemeris-type table for December (about 32 daily rows, with a final column near 1.31). Its right margin repeats the epochs 1817/1818.0 … 1819.0. This page is a short side calculation: the nutation reduction parameters for the epochs 1818.0–1819.0 at tenth-of-a-year steps.

(1) TABLE, column 2 = longitude of the Moon's ascending node, Ω (degrees.minutes). Entries: 45°8', 43°11', 41°15', 39°19', 37°23', 35°27', 33°31', 31°35', 29°39', 27°43', 25°47'.
- The step is 1°56' per 0.1 year, i.e. a regression of about 19°20' per year. This is the node's regression of 19.341° per year.
- Check (mine): the modern mean node gives Ω(J2000) = 125.04°. Then Ω(1818.0) = 125.04° + 182 × 19.3414° = 3645.2° ≡ 45.2°, matching 45°8'.
- Over the whole year Gauss's table drops 19°21' (45°8' → 25°47'). The exact rate gives 19°20.5'. So he rounded each step to whole minutes, with one 1°57' step absorbing the accumulation.

(2) DEFINITIONS (lower part of the page). The symbol read as ⊙ in the transcription must be the node ☊; the numbers prove it.
- a = −α·sin Ω, with α = M/50 and log α = 9.52196, so α = 0.33255.
- b = −N·cos Ω, with log N = 0.95124, so N = 8.936″.
- Here 50 is the round value of the general precession p (″/yr) and M is the constant of nutation in longitude. So α = M/p, giving M ≈ 16.63″ if p = 50″ exactly.
- N is the constant of nutation in obliquity.
- In modern terms: Δψ = −M sin Ω, Δε = +N cos Ω, a = Δψ/p and b = −Δε.

(3) TABLE, columns 3–4. These are a and b for 1818.5–1819.0. Check (mine):
- 1818.5: Ω = 35°27', sin Ω = 0.5800, so a = −0.33255 × 0.5800 = −0.1929. cos Ω = 0.8146, so b = −8.936 × 0.8146 = −7.28.
- 1819.0: Ω = 25°47', a = −0.33255 × 0.4350 = −0.1447 and b = −8.936 × 0.9005 = −8.05.
- The intermediate rows agree to the last digit, apart from ±1 unit in the 4th decimal at 1818.6 and 1818.8.

(4) REDUCTION FORMULAS. Here α, δ are the star's right ascension and declination. dα = m + n sin α tan δ is the annual precession in RA and dδ = n cos α the annual precession in Dec, with m = p cos ε and n = p sin ε.
- Nut.AR = a·dα + b·tan δ·cos α
- Nut.D = a·dδ − b·sin α
- Derivation (mine). The standard first-order nutation is:
  - Δα = Δψ(cos ε + sin ε sin α tan δ) − Δε cos α tan δ
  - Δδ = Δψ sin ε cos α + Δε sin α
- Since Δψ cos ε = (Δψ/p)·m and Δψ sin ε = (Δψ/p)·n, these become:
  - Δα = (Δψ/p)·dα − Δε tan δ cos α = a·dα + b tan δ cos α
  - Δδ = (Δψ/p)·dδ + Δε sin α = a·dδ − b sin α
- This is exactly Gauss's pair. Purpose: to reduce mean places of stars to apparent places using tabulated node-dependent quantities a and b, plus each star's annual precession.

SUMMARY: a compact table of 'day numbers' for the principal (18.6-yr) nutation term over 1818, and the Bessel-type formulas for applying them.
errors: No substantive errors. The formulas agree with standard first-order nutation theory, given Δψ = −M sin Ω, Δε = N cos Ω, a = Δψ/p and b = −Δε.
Notational clash: α denotes both the constant M/50 and the star's right ascension in the same formulas. This is not a mathematical error.
Using 50″ for the general precession, instead of about 50.2″, is a deliberate rounding. It introduces a relative error of about 0.4% in a, which is negligible at this precision.
The node column has one step of 1°57' (45°8'→43°11'); all others are 1°56'. This is consistent with rounding a true rate of 1°56.05' per 0.1 yr.
Small last-digit discrepancies: at 1818.6, a = −0.1836 computed vs −0.1837 written; at 1818.8, −0.1645 vs −0.1646. These are attributable to Ω being rounded to the minute.

results.what: Tabulation of the longitude of the Moon's ascending node for 1818.0–1819.0 at 0.1-yr intervals (regression ≈19°20'/yr)
results.modern_name: Mean longitude of the lunar ascending node (fundamental argument Ω)
results.usually_credited_to: Standard almanac quantity (lunar theory, 18th c.: Mayer, Laplace, Bürg etc.)

results.what: Node-dependent nutation quantities a = −(M/p) sin Ω and b = −N cos Ω, with log(M/50) = 9.52196 and log N = 0.95124 (N = 8.936″)
results.modern_name: Besselian day numbers for nutation (the 18.6-yr principal term), cf. A, B in Bessel's reduction
results.usually_credited_to: F. W. Bessel (Fundamenta Astronomiae 1818; Tabulae Regiomontanae 1830)

results.what: Nut. in RA = a·dα + b tanδ cosα; Nut. in Dec = a·dδ − b sinα, expressing the Δψ part through the annual precession
results.modern_name: First-order nutation reduction in RA/Dec in Besselian form (star constants a, b, c, d)
results.usually_credited_to: Bessel (c. 1818–1830); the underlying formulas go back to Bradley, Euler and Lalande

deep.surprise_reason: This is routine practical astronomy of the period: day numbers for the principal nutation term and the standard (Besselian-type) reduction formulas, computed for 1818 while preparing reductions. It is contemporaneous with Bessel's Fundamenta, and Gauss as Göttingen observatory director routinely did such work. The only mildly interesting details are his adopted constants (N = 8.936″, M ≈ 16.63″ with p = 50″).

transcription_corrections: In 'sin ⊙' and 'cos ⊙' the symbol is the lunar node ☊ (Ω), not the Sun. The tabulated a, b values fit sin and cos of the column-2 node longitudes exactly.
The first epoch is written 1818.0, with a digit overwritten (the previous page's margin reads it as 1817,0). The last epoch appears as '1819 10' / '1818,10', meaning 1819.0.
Column 2 lists node longitudes in degrees.minutes (e.g. 45°8', 43°11'), not decimals.
